title: Reading Athanasius, On the Incarnation

objectives.can: Read a chapter of Athanasius: classicising periods, articular infinitives, abstract nouns and the optative.

explanation.summary: Athanasius of Alexandria wrote On the Incarnation in the fourth century (the exact date is debated). His Greek is a learned, literary Greek: long sentences built from participles, articular infinitives and abstract nouns, with the optative in places where the New Testament would not use it. This lesson reads one opening chapter slowly and sets a sentence beside the New Testament Greek you already know.

sections.heading: Before you read: the text is analysed by machine
body: The Greek of On the Incarnation in this library was analysed by a program and has not been checked by hand, and the English reference is matched only to whole chapters, not to single verses. So on this page a lemma or a grammatical label can be wrong or missing. In 3.4, for example, the program has read the infinitive ζῆν as the name Ζεύς, and in 1.4 it takes δημιουργοῦ for a verb. It reads φυλάξοιεν in 3.4 as a future optative, a form that is unusual in a condition like this one, so the lesson does not rely on it. The lesson picks examples whose analysis is reliable and writes its questions by hand. When the program and the grammar disagree, trust the grammar.

sections.heading: The chapter: why the world exists, and what went wrong
body: Chapter 3 states two things. In 3.1 God made all things 'out of what was not' (ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι), not out of pre-existing matter and not by chance. In 3.3 God, being good, begrudged no one existence, and so made human beings with a share in the power of the Word. In 3.4 and 3.5 he turns to the command given in the garden and to what he takes the words θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε to mean. The chapter is therefore a small argument, and each section answers a question the previous one raised.
You do not have to agree with a writer to read him. The aim here is the Greek: how the long sentences are built and what each form does.

sections.heading: Articular infinitives
body: A noun-like infinitive made with τό, τοῦ or τῷ is the most visible mark of this style. In 3.1 διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀπρονόητα εἶναι means 'because they are not without forethought': διά with the accusative of an articular infinitive gives a reason. εἰς τὸ εἶναι is 'into being'. In 3.2 εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι gives the aim or the result of what precedes ('so that what is seen has not come from things that appear'); grammarians describe this construction in both ways.

The genitive form is used after certain verbs. In 3.3 οὐδενὶ τοῦ εἶναι φθονήσας is 'having begrudged no one existence': verbs of envy take a genitive of the thing begrudged, and the genitive here is an articular infinitive. In 3.5, τὸ μὴ μόνον ἀποθνήσκειν ἀλλὰ καὶ … διαμένειν treats a pair of infinitives as a single noun, 'the not only dying but also remaining'.

sections.heading: The optative
body: The New Testament has only a few optatives. Athanasius has many, as the Atticising writers of his time did. He uses two kinds in this chapter. First, a potential optative with ἄν: ἀγαθῷ δὲ περὶ οὐδενὸς ἂν γένοιτο φθόνος (3.3), 'in one who is good no envy about anything could arise'. The same pattern appears in the question τί ἂν ἄλλο εἴη ἢ …; (3.5), 'what else could it be than …?'.

Second, a verb in the optative because the writer is reporting a thought from a past point of view. In 3.3 θεωρήσας ὡς οὐχ ἱκανὸν εἴη …, 'seeing that it would not be enough …', has εἴη in the optative after a past narrative. In 3.4 the two conditions that God sets in the garden are stated with optatives (εἰ μὲν … μένοιεν; εἰ δὲ παραβαῖεν … γινώσκοιεν); a New Testament writer would more likely have used a subjunctive or an indicative. This is the learned, classical style, not the everyday Greek of the Gospels.

sections.heading: Chains of participles and abstract nouns
body: The first sentence of 3.4 shows the periodic structure. Participles lead (εἰδώς, 'knowing …', then προλαβών, 'having taken precautions first'), and a single finite verb, ἠσφαλίσατο, 'he made secure', closes the clause. Find the finite verb first, then fit the participles round it.

The vocabulary is full of abstract nouns, such as ἀγαθότητος (3.3), φθορά, 'corruption' (3.4, 3.5), ἀφθαρσίας and φύσις, 'nature'. The edition spells Λόγου with a capital in τοῦ ἰδίου Λόγου; that capital is the editor's reading. In κατὰ τὸν τῆς ἰδίας γενέσεως λόγον (3.3) the word is spelled with a small letter and means something like 'the account or principle of its own coming-to-be'. The range of λόγος is the subject of a later lesson.

sections.heading: Scripture inside the argument
body: Athanasius cites Scripture as part of his argument. In 3.1 he introduces Genesis 1:1 with διὰ μὲν Μωυσέως, 'through Moses'. In 3.2 he cites Paul with φησί: Πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. These are the words of Hebrews 11:3, which many ancient writers took to be Paul's; the letter itself names no author, and modern scholars usually leave the authorship open. Set the two passages side by side: they differ in one phrase. Athanasius has τὰ βλεπόμενα (plural), where Hebrews has τὸ βλεπόμενον (singular). Such small differences are normal in ancient quotation from memory or from another manuscript tradition.

misunderstandings: An articular infinitive is not a gerund with 'the'. τὸ εἶναι is a noun, 'being' or 'existence', and its case shows its job in the sentence: accusative after διά ('because …'), genitive after φθονέω.
ἄν with an optative is not a wish. γένοιτο alone could express a wish ('may it happen'); with ἄν it says what could happen.
Not every optative in Athanasius is potential. Check whether ἄν is there, and whether the verb sits in a report of someone's thought.
Do not trust every label in the analysis. The program mistakes some forms of ζῆν and some nouns for verbs; check the grammar.

deeper.heading: Atticising Greek
body: From the late first century BC onward, many educated writers tried to write Greek like the prose of classical Athens: they kept the optative, wrote ἄν carefully and used long periodic sentences. The New Testament is nearer to the everyday Greek of its time. Athanasius sits between: he is a Christian bishop writing in a literate, Atticising register. When you see an optative in a late author, ask whether it follows classical rules; it usually does.

examples.analysis: Three articular infinitives. διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀπρονόητα εἶναι (focus 27): the infinitive εἶναι with the article after διά, 'because they are not without forethought'. διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀσθενῆ εἶναι τὸν Θεόν (focus 36): the same construction, with τὸν Θεόν as the accusative subject of εἶναι, 'because God is not weak'. εἰς τὸ εἶναι (focus 51): 'into being'. Then πεποιηκέναι, a perfect active infinitive: 'to have made'. Many of the neighbouring words are not analysed by the program.

quoted.reference: Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione Verbi) 3.2
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: Πίστει is a dative of means, 'by faith'. νοοῦμεν is a present indicative, first person plural: 'we perceive'. The two infinitives that follow are its object in indirect statement: κατηρτίσθαι, a perfect passive infinitive, 'that the ages have been fitted together', and γεγονέναι, a perfect infinitive, in the articular phrase εἰς τὸ μὴ … γεγονέναι. The sentence is a quotation of Hebrews 11:3.

examples.analysis: ἂν γένοιτο is a potential optative: aorist optative, third person singular, with ἄν. The subject is φθόνος, 'envy', and the sentence says that in one who is good envy 'could not arise'. εἶναι, in οὐδενὶ τοῦ εἶναι φθονήσας, is the infinitive after the genitive article: what is not begrudged. εἴη is a present optative, third person singular, of εἰμί, inside a clause that reports the thought of God: ὡς οὐχ ἱκανὸν εἴη, 'that it would not be enough'.

examples.analysis: προλαβών is an aorist participle, and ἠσφαλίσατο is the finite verb it modifies: 'having taken precautions first, he made secure (the grace given to them)'. The conditions that follow use optatives: μένοιεν, a present optative, 'if they were to remain', παραβαῖεν, an aorist optative, 'if they were to transgress', and γινώσκοιεν, 'they would know'. Notice how different this is from the subjunctives of the New Testament conditions you studied. The first verb of the first condition, φυλάξοιεν, is left out of this list because its analysis is doubtful.

check.explain: The phrase belongs to the reasoning about what the human race would be by its own origin. The edition keeps the capital Λόγος for the Word in τοῦ ἰδίου Λόγου, but here the word is written with a small letter.

reading.why: Three sections of one chapter in which the lesson's features recur: articular infinitives, a potential optative with ἄν, optatives in reported conditions, chains of participles and abstract nouns, and a citation of Scripture. Read for the finite verbs first. The program's analysis is automatic and sometimes wrong.
